planting.note: Set rhizome divisions shallowly into living sphagnum or a peat-sand bog mix after the last hard frost, keeping the crown at the surface and the root zone constantly saturated.

directions: This federally endangered pitcher plant is restricted to a handful of mountain seepage bogs in the Blue Ridge of North and South Carolina, a cooler and higher-elevation home than most Sarracenia tolerate. Narrow, erect yellow-green to coppery pitchers have a tightly arching, non-flaring hood that sheds rain while still luring and trapping insects, and nodding maroon flowers open on separate stalks in spring before the new pitchers unfurl. Grow it exactly as its native seep demands: year-round saturated, acidic, nutrient-starved peat or sphagrass, full sun, and only rainwater or distilled water, since minerals and fertilizer quickly kill the roots. It is a centerpiece plant for an outdoor bog container or constructed bog garden rather than a border perennial.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service recovery plan

planting.note: Divide and reset rhizomes in spring into a wet, acidic peat-sand bog mix; keep the crown just above the surface and never let the medium dry out.

directions: A federally endangered pitcher plant once scattered through open, sunlit seepage bogs within and alongside Alabama canebrakes near the Cahaba River drainage, now reduced to a small number of sites. Its slender, somewhat erect pitchers are heavily veined with maroon on green, more upright and less trumpet-flared than the showier coastal species, and nodding spring flowers open a deep wine-red before the season's pitchers mature. Like its relatives it demands the paradox conditions of a true bog: full sun, constant moisture, strongly acidic peat, and essentially no dissolved minerals, so grow it in a dedicated bog tray or planted peat bed watered only with rain or distilled water. Winter dormancy with cut-back, blackened pitchers is normal and should not be mistaken for decline.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service recovery plan

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall at normal bulb depth in sandy or rocky, consistently damp soil; the grasslike foliage emerges over winter and the plant goes summer-dormant after bloom.

directions: Sunnybell is a diminutive bulb of seasonally wet glades, limestone and sandstone seeps, and pine flatwoods across the south-central and southeastern US, including the shallow-soil limestone glades of the Ozark and Ouachita region. A tight tuft of narrow, grasslike leaves sends up a slender scape carrying a loose cluster of small, bright golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers in early-to-mid spring, after which the whole plant disappears underground for the summer. Because it naturally straddles open glade edges and lightly shaded flatwoods margins, it tolerates part shade better than most glade bulbs and resents being dried out completely during its brief growing season. Best used at the damp edge of a rock garden, glade restoration, or seasonally wet meadow where its dormancy will not be missed once summer heat arrives.

planting.note: Plant root-sprout divisions or container stock in spring into lean, sandy or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; isolate from aggressive turf, since the colony spreads by root suckers.

directions: A federally endangered dwarf sumac of the southeastern Piedmont and sandhills, Michaux's sumac forms low, suckering colonies on dry, infertile sandy or rocky openings such as granite outcrop margins and longleaf pine-wiregrass woodlands that historically stayed open through frequent fire. It is dioecious, with separate male and female plants producing upright, densely hairy flower panicles in early summer; only females follow with clusters of small red, fuzzy fruit that persist into winter and feed birds when little else is available. Its low, spreading habit and tolerance of poor, droughty soil make it useful for restoring open sandy sites, but it needs full sun and occasional disturbance or mowing to keep taller woody competitors from shading it out. Give it room, since a healthy colony will sucker well beyond its original planting spot.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service recovery plan

planting.note: Tuck small plants or seed into shallow pockets of sharply draining, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; established roots are easily damaged, so avoid transplanting large specimens.

directions: Menges' fameflower is a tiny succulent of thin soil pockets on exposed granite and gneiss outcrops across the southern Appalachian Piedmont, rooted in the same kind of flatrock microhabitat that also hosts rare Diamorpha and quillwort communities. Fleshy, cylindrical leaves form a loose low rosette, and on sunny summer afternoons each plant opens a few delicate, five-petaled pink-to-rose flowers that last only a few hours before closing for the day. Because its native perch dries to the point of baking in summer and floods briefly after rain, it needs sharp drainage above all else; a standard garden bed will rot the roots. It is best suited to a rock garden crevice, outcrop simulation, or trough planting that mimics the lean, gritty, periodically saturated-then-bone-dry conditions of its outcrop home.

planting.note: Install plugs or divisions in spring into sandy, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; plan on periodic mowing or burning in subsequent years to trigger flowering and keep the stand vigorous.

directions: Wiregrass is the dominant groundcover bunchgrass of fire-maintained longleaf pine savannas on the Atlantic coastal plain, forming dense, fine-textured tussocks of wiry blue-green leaves that carpet the open understory between widely spaced pines. It is tightly bound to fire ecology: without burning on something close to its historic one-to-three-year interval it rarely flowers, builds up thatch, and slowly loses vigor, so plantings intended to flower and seed need a mowing or controlled-burn regimen rather than a one-time planting. Narrow, inconspicuous flower spikes appear in fall following a spring or summer fire. It thrives in the same lean, droughty, sandy soil that would starve most ornamental grasses and is used almost exclusively in longleaf ecosystem restoration rather than conventional landscaping.

planting.note: Direct sow or set transplants into sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in fall or spring; a basal rosette of felted leaves persists through winter before the flowering stalk rises in late summer.

directions: This southeastern coastal plain native grows scattered through dry sandhills, open pinelands, and flatwoods, forming a low rosette of gray-green leaves covered in a soft wool-like fuzz that distinguishes it from its smoother-leaved relative, the vanilla plant. In late summer and fall the rosette sends up a single flowering stalk topped with a rounded cluster of lavender-purple disk flowers that draw in bees, skippers, and migrating butterflies working the sandhill before frost. It is well adapted to the periodic fire and mowing that keep sandhill habitat open, since too much shade or unchecked woody growth will crowd it out over a few seasons. Give it lean, sandy, acidic soil and full sun, and skip supplemental fertilizer, which pushes floppy growth at the expense of the tidy basal rosette.
